title: Evaluating Trust in AI, Human, and Co-produced Feedback Among Undergraduate Students
extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students perceive and trust formative feedback when it is generated by three different sources: AI alone, human teaching assistants, and human-AI co-produced feedback. The core problem is that while large language models are increasingly used to generate educational feedback in higher education, student adoption may depend not only on feedback quality but also on whether students trust the source and react differently once the source is disclosed. The study asks what predicts students’ ability to identify AI feedback, how perceptions change when feedback sources are revealed, and what biases students hold toward AI, human, and co-produced feedback.

The approach was a within-subject online experimental survey in which students viewed their own assignment responses alongside three feedback variants: human feedback from teaching assistants, AI-generated feedback from Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and co-produced feedback in which AI revised TA feedback. Students first rated the feedback blind on usefulness, objectivity, and genuineness, then completed AI trust measures, attempted to identify which feedback was AI or co-produced, and finally re-rated the feedback after the source labels were revealed, including source credibility ratings. Analyses used logistic regression and mixed linear models to examine associations between student characteristics, perceptions, and credibility judgments.

The study involved 91 first- and second-year psychology students at a UK university, with 82 usable responses included in analysis after missing data and exclusions. The context was authentic higher education coursework in statistics classes over five weeks, using challenging assignment questions on chi-square analysis and factor analysis. Teaching assistants normally provided feedback as part of course practice, and AI-generated and co-produced feedback were created from the same student submissions for comparison.

The main findings were that, when sources were hidden, students generally rated AI and co-produced feedback as more useful and more objective than human feedback. Once sources were revealed, students showed a clear credibility bias against AI-only feedback: human and co-produced feedback were rated more credible than AI feedback, and AI feedback alone declined in perceived genuineness. Students with more educational AI experience were better able to identify AI-generated feedback and tended to rate feedback as more credible overall, whereas more years of general AI use were associated with lower usefulness and credibility ratings. The authors conclude that source framing strongly shapes trust in educational AI, and that co-produced feedback may be a practical middle ground because it preserves positive student perceptions while leveraging AI support.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's large language model family used here to generate formative feedback and to revise teaching-assistant feedback into co-produced feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Claude 3.5 Sonnet was selected and used via API to generate AI feedback on undergraduate statistics assignments and to improve TA-written feedback for a human-AI co-produced feedback condition, which was then compared with human-only feedback in a within-subject experiment.

findings.finding_summary: In blind ratings, students rated AI feedback higher than human feedback across objectivity, usefulness, and genuineness, and co-produced feedback was also rated higher than human feedback across all dimensions (all p < .05 for AI vs human; all p < .001 for co-produced vs human). Means were Objectivity: AI MBlind=4.11 vs Human MBlind=3.31; Usefulness: AI MBlind=4.12 vs Human MBlind=3.17; Genuineness: AI MBlind=4.11 vs Human MBlind=3.19; n=82.
findings.measure: Student perceptions of feedback quality: objectivity, usefulness, genuineness on 5-point Likert scales

findings.finding_summary: When feedback source was revealed, only AI feedback showed a significant decline in perceived genuineness, while co-produced and human feedback remained stable. AI genuineness dropped from MBlind=4.11 to MInformed=3.67 (p < .001); the main effect of timing was significant only for genuineness (p < .001); n=82.
findings.measure: Perceived genuineness of feedback before vs after source disclosure

findings.finding_summary: Students rated AI feedback as significantly less credible than human and co-produced feedback after disclosure. Credibility means were Human M=4.18, SD=0.84; AI M=3.28, SD=0.84; Co-produced M=4.04, SD=0.69, with Human vs AI p < .001, Cohen's d=1.21, and Co-produced vs AI p < .001, Cohen's d=1.02; n=82.
findings.measure: Perceived credibility of feedback provider (trustworthy, reliable, ethical)

findings.finding_summary: Years of educational AI usage significantly predicted students' ability to correctly identify AI-generated feedback in the simplified Turing test. The association was significant for AI feedback identification (χ2=4.08, p=.028) but not for co-produced feedback identification (χ2=0.64, p=.802); n=82.
findings.measure: Ability to identify AI-generated and co-produced feedback sources

findings.finding_summary: More years of educational AI usage predicted higher credibility ratings for feedback (p=.027, β=0.27), while more years of general AI usage predicted lower credibility ratings (p=.025, β=-0.27). Higher perceived usefulness in the AI trust instrument also predicted higher credibility ratings specifically for AI-generated feedback (p=.019, β=0.30); n=82.
findings.measure: Credibility ratings as predicted by AI experience and AI trust measures

findings.finding_summary: More years of general AI usage were associated with lower usefulness ratings for feedback overall (p=.024, β=-0.36). Male participants also rated usefulness lower than female/non-binary participants, with a significant interaction showing lower usefulness ratings for human feedback among male students (M=2.67 vs 3.46, p=.001); n=82.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical within-subject experimental study with n=82 analyzed participants, but it focuses on perceptions, trust, and source disclosure effects rather than randomized learning outcome impacts. The design is stronger than purely descriptive work, yet it is not an RCT/QED on student achievement.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large perception effects against disclosed AI on credibility, including Cohen's d=1.21 and d=1.02 for credibility comparisons. Although impacts are attitudinal rather than academic achievement effects, the reported magnitudes are substantial.
